Question: Infrastructure as a service (IaaS) (cloud architecture)
Answer: the provider runs the physical hardware, network and hypervisor. You get virtual machines, virtual networks and block storage, and you run the operating system and everything above it. AWS EC2, Azure Virtual Machines and Google Compute Engine are IaaS.

Question: Platform as a service (PaaS) (cloud architecture)
Answer: the provider also runs the operating system, middleware and runtime. You deploy code and manage data. Azure App Service, AWS Elastic Beanstalk and Google App Engine are PaaS.

Question: Software as a service (SaaS) (cloud architecture)
Answer: the provider runs the whole application. You configure it and manage users and data. Microsoft 365, Salesforce and Google Workspace are SaaS.

Question: Function as a service (FaaS) (cloud architecture)
Answer: you upload a function and the provider runs it when an event fires. You pay per invocation and execution time, and you never see a server. AWS Lambda, Azure Functions and Google Cloud Run functions are FaaS.

Question: Region (cloud architecture)
Answer: a geographic area containing several data centres. Regions are independent of each other, so a regional outage does not spread. You pick a region for latency to users, data residency law, service availability and price.

Question: Availability zone (AZ) (cloud architecture)
Answer: one or more data centres inside a region with independent power, cooling and networking, linked by low-latency connections. Spreading instances across AZs protects you from a single data-centre failure without the latency cost of going cross-region.

Question: Cloud bursting (cloud architecture)
Answer: running normally in a private data centre and overflowing to public cloud when demand exceeds local capacity. It needs compatible images, network connectivity and usually an orchestration layer that knows when to burst.

Question: Edge computing (cloud architecture)
Answer: running compute close to where data is created or consumed, such as a factory floor, a retail store or a CDN point of presence. It cuts latency and reduces how much raw data travels back to a region.

Question: Availability monitoring (cloud architecture)
Answer: checking from outside that a service actually answers. Synthetic checks (a probe that loads a page every minute from several locations) catch failures that internal metrics miss, such as a DNS or certificate problem.

Question: Recovery time objective (RTO) (cloud architecture)
Answer: the maximum acceptable time from the failure to service being restored. It is about downtime.

Question: Recovery point objective (RPO) (cloud architecture)
Answer: the maximum acceptable data loss, measured in time back from the failure. An RPO of 15 minutes means backups or replication must capture changes at least every 15 minutes.

Question: Hot site (cloud architecture)
Answer: a fully running duplicate environment with current data. Failover takes minutes or less. Highest cost.

Question: Warm site (cloud architecture)
Answer: infrastructure is in place and partly running, data is fairly recent, but it needs scaling up and some configuration before it can take full load. Hours.

Question: Cold site (cloud architecture)
Answer: space, power and maybe network, but no running systems and no current data. You restore from backup. Days. Lowest cost.

Question: Virtual private network (VPN) (cloud architecture)
Answer: an encrypted tunnel over the public internet. A site-to-site VPN joins an office or data centre network to a cloud virtual network, usually with IPsec. A client (remote access) VPN connects a single user. VPNs are quick to set up and cheap, but bandwidth and latency depend on the internet path.

Question: Dedicated connection (cloud architecture)
Answer: a private circuit from your premises or a colocation facility into the provider's network. AWS calls this Direct Connect, Azure calls it ExpressRoute, Google calls it Cloud Interconnect. It gives predictable bandwidth and latency and avoids the internet, but it takes weeks to provision and costs more. It is not encrypted by default, so some designs run a VPN over it.

Question: Application load balancer (cloud architecture)
Answer: works at Layer 7. It reads HTTP, so it can route by path (/api to one group, /images to another) or host header, terminate TLS and insert headers.

Question: Network load balancer (cloud architecture)
Answer: works at Layer 4 (TCP and UDP). It does not look inside the request, so it handles very high throughput with very low latency, supports non-HTTP protocols and can keep a static IP.

Question: Application gateway (cloud architecture)
Answer: a Layer 7 reverse proxy that often combines load balancing, TLS termination and a web application firewall. Azure uses this exact name. In other clouds the same job is done by an application load balancer plus a WAF, or by an API gateway for API traffic.

Question: Content delivery network (CDN) (cloud architecture)
Answer: a global network of edge caches that serve static content close to users. It reduces latency, offloads the origin and absorbs some DDoS traffic.

Question: Firewall (cloud architecture)
Answer: filters traffic by rules. In cloud you meet stateful instance-level rules (security groups), stateless subnet-level rules (network ACLs) and managed firewall appliances for inspection between networks.

Question: Virtual private cloud (VPC) (cloud architecture)
Answer: your logically isolated network in a provider, with your own IP range, subnets and route tables. Azure calls it a virtual network (VNet).

Question: VPC peering (cloud architecture)
Answer: a private, direct link between two VPCs. It is not transitive: if A peers with B and B peers with C, A cannot reach C through B.

Question: Transit gateway (cloud architecture)
Answer: a regional hub that many VPCs and VPN or dedicated connections attach to. It replaces a mesh of peering links with hub and spoke, and it supports transitive routing through its own route tables. Azure's equivalent is Virtual WAN or a hub VNet; Google uses Network Connectivity Center.

Question: Subnet (cloud architecture)
Answer: a slice of the VPC's address range, usually tied to one availability zone. A public subnet has a route to an internet gateway. A private subnet does not, and reaches the internet (if at all) through a NAT gateway.

Question: Virtual local area network (VLAN) (cloud architecture)
Answer: a Layer 2 broadcast domain separated by a tag (802.1Q) on the frames. VLANs segment traffic on shared switches. In private clouds and on-premises virtualization you still configure VLANs directly.

Question: Software-defined network (SDN) (cloud architecture)
Answer: networking where the control plane (decisions) is separated from the data plane (forwarding) and managed centrally through software and APIs. Every public cloud VPC is SDN, which is why you can create a network with an API call.

Question: Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) (cloud architecture)
Answer: the routing protocol that exchanges routes between autonomous systems. Dedicated connections and many VPNs use BGP so routes are learned dynamically and failover happens automatically.

Question: Static route (cloud architecture)
Answer: a route typed in by hand. Simple and predictable, but it does not react to failures.

Question: Route table (cloud architecture)
Answer: the list of destinations and next hops attached to a subnet. The most specific matching prefix wins.

Question: Hot tier (cloud architecture)
Answer: frequently accessed data. Highest storage price per GB, lowest access cost and latency.

Question: Warm tier (cloud architecture)
Answer: accessed occasionally, perhaps monthly. Cheaper to store, with a per-access charge and sometimes a minimum storage duration.

Question: Cold tier (cloud architecture)
Answer: rarely accessed, perhaps a few times a year. Cheaper again, with higher retrieval charges.

Question: Archive tier (cloud architecture)
Answer: kept for compliance or history. Very cheap to store, but retrieval can take hours and costs the most. AWS S3 Glacier Deep Archive, Azure Archive and Google Archive storage are examples.

Question: Solid-state drive (SSD) (cloud architecture)
Answer: no moving parts, high IOPS and low latency. The default for boot volumes and databases.

Question: Hard disk drive (HDD) (cloud architecture)
Answer: spinning media, cheap per GB, good sequential throughput but poor random IOPS. Fits large sequential workloads such as log processing or a data warehouse staging area.

Question: Block storage (cloud architecture)
Answer: raw volumes presented to a VM as disks. The OS formats them. Lowest latency, usually attached to one instance at a time. AWS EBS, Azure Managed Disks, Google Persistent Disk.

Question: File storage (cloud architecture)
Answer: a shared file system over NFS or SMB that many machines can mount at once. Good for shared content and lift-and-shift apps that expect a network drive. AWS EFS and FSx, Azure Files, Google Filestore.

Question: Object storage (cloud architecture)
Answer: objects in flat buckets, accessed over HTTP APIs, with metadata and practically unlimited scale. Cheapest per GB and very durable, but you cannot mount it as a normal disk or edit part of an object in place. AWS S3, Azure Blob Storage, Google Cloud Storage.

Question: Cloud-provided managed services (cloud architecture)
Answer: databases, queues, caches and identity that the provider runs and patches. You trade some control for much less operational work and built-in high availability.

Question: Microservices (cloud architecture)
Answer: an application split into small services, each owning one business capability and its own data, deployed independently. The benefit is independent scaling and release. The cost is more network calls, distributed debugging and the need for good observability.

Question: Loosely coupled architecture (cloud architecture)
Answer: components talk through queues, events or stable APIs instead of direct, synchronous calls. If one component slows down or fails, the others keep working and the queue absorbs the backlog.

Question: Fan-out (cloud architecture)
Answer: one message is delivered to many consumers in parallel, for example a "new order" event going to billing, shipping and analytics. A publish-subscribe topic feeding several queues is the classic pattern (AWS SNS to SQS, Azure Service Bus topics, Google Pub/Sub).

Question: Service discovery (cloud architecture)
Answer: how services find each other when instances come and go. A registry or DNS-based system keeps the current address list, so callers ask "where is the payments service?" instead of hard-coding IPs. Kubernetes Services, AWS Cloud Map and Consul do this.

Question: Stand-alone containers (cloud architecture)
Answer: containers run directly on one host by a runtime such as Docker. Fine for development, simple tools or a single small service. Nothing restarts them on another host if this host dies.

Question: Workload orchestration (cloud architecture)
Answer: a platform that schedules containers across a cluster, restarts failed ones, scales replicas, rolls out updates and handles service discovery. Kubernetes is the standard. Managed versions are Amazon EKS, Azure AKS and Google GKE. Simpler provider-specific options include Amazon ECS and serverless containers such as AWS Fargate, Azure Container Apps and Google Cloud Run.

Question: Port mapping (cloud architecture)
Answer: publishing a container's internal port on the host, for example host 8080 to container 80 (docker run -p 8080:80). Two containers cannot both bind the same host port.

Question: Persistent volumes (cloud architecture)
Answer: storage that outlives the container, mounted from a host path, network file share or cloud block volume. Databases in containers need this.

Question: Ephemeral storage (cloud architecture)
Answer: the container's writable layer. It disappears when the container is removed. Anything written there, including logs, is lost unless shipped elsewhere.

Question: Image registry (cloud architecture)
Answer: a repository that stores and versions container images. Public registries (Docker Hub) are convenient but can carry untrusted images. Private registries (Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry) add access control and vulnerability scanning.

Question: Stand-alone host (cloud architecture)
Answer: one hypervisor host with no shared management. If it fails, its VMs go down with it.

Question: Clustering (cloud architecture)
Answer: several hosts managed as a pool with shared storage, so VMs can move between hosts (live migration) and restart on a surviving host after a failure.

Question: Cloning (cloud architecture)
Answer: copying a VM to create a new one quickly. Clones of Windows machines need a fresh identity (sysprep) so they do not share security identifiers. Templates are the managed version of this idea.

Question: Host affinity (cloud architecture)
Answer: rules that keep VMs together on the same host (affinity, for low latency between them) or apart on different hosts (anti-affinity, so one host failure does not take down both members of a cluster). Licensing rules sometimes require affinity to specific hosts.

Question: Hardware pass-through (cloud architecture)
Answer: giving a VM direct access to a physical device such as a GPU or NIC (PCI pass-through, SR-IOV). It delivers near-native performance but ties the VM to that host, which can block live migration.

Question: Overlay networks (cloud architecture)
Answer: virtual networks built on top of the physical network by encapsulating traffic (VXLAN, Geneve). They let VMs or containers on different hosts share a logical network without reconfiguring physical switches. Cloud VPCs and Kubernetes pod networks are overlays.

Question: VM networks (cloud architecture)
Answer: the virtual switches and port groups that connect VMs on a host to each other and to physical uplinks, often mapped to VLANs.

Question: Local storage (cloud architecture)
Answer: disks inside the host. Fast and cheap, but VMs on it cannot live-migrate and are lost if the host is lost.

Question: Storage area network (SAN) (cloud architecture)
Answer: block storage shared over a dedicated network (Fibre Channel or iSCSI). Hosts see LUNs as local disks. It enables clustering and live migration.

Question: Network-attached storage (NAS) (cloud architecture)
Answer: file storage shared over the normal network (NFS or SMB).

Question: Dedicated host (cloud architecture)
Answer: a whole physical server reserved for you. The most expensive option, chosen for per-socket or per-core software licensing (bring your own licence) or compliance that forbids shared hardware.

Question: Reserved resources (cloud architecture)
Answer: a one or three year commitment in exchange for a large discount, often 40 to 70 percent. Best for steady, predictable baseload. Savings plans are a more flexible form.

Question: Pay-as-you-go (cloud architecture)
Answer: on-demand pricing billed per second or hour with no commitment. Highest unit price, full flexibility. Right for new, short-lived or unpredictable workloads.

Question: Spot instance (cloud architecture)
Answer: spare capacity at up to around 90 percent off, which the provider can reclaim with very short notice (two minutes on AWS, 30 seconds on Azure and Google). Right for fault-tolerant, interruptible work such as batch, rendering and CI runners. Wrong for a primary database.

Question: Resource metering (cloud architecture)
Answer: measuring usage per resource (hours, GB, requests, GB transferred) so billing reflects consumption. Metering data is what chargeback and showback reports are built from.

Question: Tagging (cloud architecture)
Answer: key-value labels such as CostCenter=Finance or Environment=Prod. Tags let you split the bill by team or project and find orphaned resources. A tagging policy only works if it is enforced at creation time.

Question: Rightsizing (cloud architecture)
Answer: matching instance size to actual use. A VM averaging 8 percent CPU is a rightsizing candidate. Rightsize before you buy reservations, or you lock in waste for three years.

Question: Relational database (cloud architecture)
Answer: data in tables with a fixed schema, related by keys and queried with SQL. Strong consistency and ACID transactions. Fits orders, payments and anything where correctness of related records matters. MySQL, PostgreSQL, SQL Server, Oracle.

Question: Non-relational (NoSQL) database (cloud architecture)
Answer: flexible or no schema, designed to scale out horizontally. Families include key-value (DynamoDB, Redis), document (MongoDB, Cosmos DB), wide-column (Cassandra, Bigtable) and graph (Neo4j). Fits high-volume, simple-access-pattern or rapidly changing data such as sessions, catalogues and IoT readings.

Question: Self-managed (cloud architecture)
Answer: you install and run the database on a VM or container. Full control of version, extensions and tuning; you also own patching, backups, replication and failover.

Question: Provider-managed (cloud architecture)
Answer: database as a service (Amazon RDS and Aurora, Azure SQL Database, Google Cloud SQL, DynamoDB). The provider handles patching, backups, multi-AZ failover and scaling options. Less control of the underlying OS.

Question: Text recognition (cloud architecture)
Answer: optical character recognition (OCR) that extracts printed or handwritten text from images and documents. AWS Textract, Azure AI Document Intelligence, Google Document AI.

Question: Text translation (cloud architecture)
Answer: machine translation between languages. AWS Translate, Azure AI Translator, Google Cloud Translation.

Question: Visual recognition (cloud architecture)
Answer: detecting objects, faces, scenes or unsafe content in images and video. AWS Rekognition, Azure AI Vision, Google Cloud Vision.

Question: Sentiment analysis (cloud architecture)
Answer: judging whether text is positive, negative or neutral, for example in product reviews or support tickets. AWS Comprehend, Azure AI Language.

Question: Voice-to-text (cloud architecture)
Answer: speech recognition that turns audio into a transcript. AWS Transcribe, Azure AI Speech, Google Speech-to-Text.

Question: Text-to-voice (cloud architecture)
Answer: speech synthesis that reads text aloud in a natural voice. AWS Polly, Azure AI Speech, Google Text-to-Speech.

Question: Generative AI (cloud architecture)
Answer: large models that create new text, code or images from a prompt. Delivered through managed platforms such as Amazon Bedrock, Azure OpenAI Service and Google Vertex AI. Key cloud concerns are data privacy (does the prompt leave your boundary?), cost per token and output review.

Question: Sensors (cloud architecture)
Answer: small devices that measure the physical world, such as temperature, vibration or location.

Question: Gateways (cloud architecture)
Answer: local devices that collect sensor data, translate protocols, filter and buffer, then forward to the cloud. A gateway is often where edge computing happens.

Question: Communication (cloud architecture)
Answer: how devices connect: Wi-Fi, cellular, Bluetooth Low Energy, Zigbee or low-power wide-area networks such as LoRaWAN.

Question: Transmission protocols (cloud architecture)
Answer: lightweight messaging protocols such as MQTT (publish-subscribe, small overhead, the most common IoT protocol), CoAP and AMQP, plus HTTPS where devices are less constrained.

Question: Public cloud (deployment)
Answer: infrastructure owned and run by a provider and shared by many customers (multi-tenant). No capital outlay, near-unlimited scale, pay for what you use. Less control over the physical layer, and data sits in someone else's facility.

Question: Private cloud (deployment)
Answer: cloud-style self-service and automation on infrastructure used by one organization only. It may be on premises (you own the data centre and hardware) or hosted (a third party runs dedicated hardware for you). Full control and isolation, but you pay for capacity whether you use it or not, and you need the staff to run it.

Question: On premises (deployment)
Answer: the private cloud variant in your own building. CompTIA calls it out because the exam distinguishes "private cloud you run" from "private cloud someone hosts".

Question: Hybrid cloud (deployment)
Answer: two or more distinct clouds (usually private plus public) connected so data and applications can move between them. Typical drivers are keeping regulated data on premises while using public cloud for burst capacity or new services, and gradual migration.

Question: Community cloud (deployment)
Answer: shared by several organizations with common concerns such as a mission, security requirements or regulation. Government agencies, a hospital group or a research consortium are typical. Costs are spread among members.

Question: Blue-green (deployment)
Answer: two identical environments. Blue runs the current version. You deploy the new version to green, test it, then switch all traffic (usually at the load balancer or DNS). Rollback is switching back. It needs double capacity during the cutover and careful handling of database schema changes that both versions must tolerate.

Question: Canary (deployment)
Answer: release the new version to a small slice of traffic or users (say 5 percent), watch error rates and latency, then widen in steps. If metrics degrade, route the canary traffic back. It limits blast radius and tests with real users, but it needs good monitoring and traffic-splitting.

Question: Rolling (deployment)
Answer: replace instances in batches, for example 25 percent at a time, while the rest keep serving. No extra capacity is needed, but for a while two versions run side by side, and rollback means rolling the old version back out batch by batch.

Question: In-place (deployment)
Answer: stop the application on existing servers, install the new version, start it again. Cheapest and simplest, but it causes downtime and the rollback is a reinstall. Acceptable for internal tools and maintenance windows.

Question: On-premises to cloud (deployment)
Answer: the classic migration. You move workloads out of your data centre.

Question: Cloud to on-premises (deployment)
Answer: repatriation. It happens when cloud cost for a steady, heavy workload exceeds owning hardware, when regulation changes, or when latency to on-premises systems matters.

Question: Cloud to cloud (deployment)
Answer: moving between providers or between regions or accounts of one provider. Drivers include cost, a service only another provider offers, mergers and avoiding lock-in.

Question: Storage (deployment)
Answer: how much data, how fast it changes and how long the transfer will take. Large datasets may need an offline transfer device (AWS Snowball, Azure Data Box) followed by online sync of changes.

Question: Platform compatibility (deployment)
Answer: OS versions, CPU architecture, hypervisor formats and licences supported by the target. An old 32-bit OS or an unsupported database version can block a rehost.

Question: Compute (deployment)
Answer: instance families that match the workload profile (general, compute-optimized, memory-optimized, GPU).

Question: Cost (deployment)
Answer: not only running cost but transfer cost, dual running during cutover, licences and staff time. Data egress charges are a common surprise in cloud to cloud and cloud to on-premises moves.

Question: Networking (deployment)
Answer: bandwidth for the transfer, connectivity back to remaining on-premises systems, IP addressing that must not overlap, and DNS changes at cutover.

Question: Management overhead (deployment)
Answer: who will run the new environment and what tooling changes.

Question: Service availability (deployment)
Answer: whether the services you need exist in the target region or provider.

Question: Vendor lock-in (deployment)
Answer: deep use of proprietary managed services makes future moves harder. It is a trade, not a sin: managed services save effort now.

Question: Environmental: power and cooling (deployment)
Answer: for a move to on premises, the data centre must have the power, cooling and floor space for the new hardware. For a move to cloud, retiring a data centre frees these costs and is part of the business case.

Question: Regulatory and compliance (deployment)
Answer: data residency, industry rules (PCI DSS, HIPAA) and contractual obligations decide which regions and services are allowed.

Question: Rehost (deployment)
Answer: lift and shift. Move the VM as-is to IaaS. Fastest, least change, least cloud benefit. Good for a deadline such as a data centre lease ending.

Question: Replatform (deployment)
Answer: lift, tinker and shift. Small changes to gain a cloud benefit without rewriting, such as moving a self-managed database to a managed database service, or a web app onto PaaS.

Question: Refactor (deployment)
Answer: change the code to fit the cloud better, for example extracting a component into a function or making the app stateless so it can scale out.

Question: Re-architect (deployment)
Answer: a deeper redesign, such as breaking a monolith into microservices or moving to event-driven design. Most effort, most cloud-native benefit. Many sources treat refactor and re-architect as one; CompTIA lists both, with re-architect as the bigger structural change.

Question: Retain (deployment)
Answer: keep it where it is for now, perhaps because it was recently upgraded, has hard latency ties to on-premises systems or cannot legally move.

Question: Retire (deployment)
Answer: switch it off. Discovery often finds applications nobody uses.

Question: Infrastructure as code (IaC) (deployment)
Answer: describing infrastructure (networks, VMs, databases, load balancers) in files that a tool reads to create and update real resources. Terraform, AWS CloudFormation, Azure Bicep and ARM templates, and Pulumi are IaC tools.

Question: Configuration as code (CaC) (deployment)
Answer: describing the configuration inside systems (packages installed, files present, services running, settings applied) in files that a tool enforces. Ansible, Chef, Puppet and PowerShell DSC are CaC tools.

Question: Variables (deployment)
Answer: named values that make code reusable, such as region = "us-east-1" or $instanceCount = 3. Hard-coded values are the opposite and a common review finding.

Question: Conditionals (deployment)
Answer: if/else logic, such as creating a second replica only when environment == "prod".

Question: Operators (deployment)
Answer: comparison (==, !=, >, <), logical (and, or, not) and arithmetic operators used inside conditionals and expressions.

Question: Data types (deployment)
Answer: strings, integers, booleans, lists (arrays) and maps (dictionaries or objects). A common error is passing a string "3" where a number is expected, or a single value where a list is required.

Question: Functions (deployment)
Answer: reusable blocks of code that take inputs and return outputs. IaC languages also ship built-in functions such as joining strings or computing subnet ranges.

Question: Repeatability (deployment)
Answer: the same code produces the same environment every time, in any region or account. This is the main reason to use IaC: dev, test and prod stay consistent.

Question: Drift detection (deployment)
Answer: comparing what the code says with what actually exists. Drift happens when someone changes a resource by hand in the console. terraform plan shows drift as planned changes; CloudFormation has a drift detection feature. The fix is to bring the change into code or let the tool revert it, then stop manual changes.

Question: Versioning (deployment)
Answer: storing templates in source control so every change has an author, a reason and a way back. Pin tool and module versions too, so an upstream update does not change your infrastructure unexpectedly.

Question: Testing (deployment)
Answer: linting and validation (terraform validate), policy checks (no public buckets, required tags), plan review and deploying to a test environment before prod.

Question: Documentation (deployment)
Answer: comments, README files and generated diagrams that explain what the code builds and why. Good IaC is partly self-documenting, but intent still needs words.

Question: JavaScript Object Notation (JSON) (deployment)
Answer: braces for objects, brackets for lists, double-quoted keys and strings, no comments allowed. Used by CloudFormation, ARM templates, IAM policies and many APIs.

Question: Storage requirements (deployment)
Answer: capacity, access pattern and sharing. Shared by many servers points to file storage. Unstructured data at scale points to object storage. A database disk points to SSD block storage.

Question: Performance requirements (deployment)
Answer: IOPS, throughput, latency and CPU or memory profile. Pick instance families and volume types to match, and place resources close to users.

Question: Security requirements (deployment)
Answer: encryption at rest and in transit, private subnets, least-privilege roles, key management. A "must not be reachable from the internet" requirement means a private subnet with no public IP.

Question: Cost requirements (deployment)
Answer: budget ceilings and pricing model. Steady workloads get reserved capacity, interruptible ones get spot, unknown ones start on demand.

Question: Availability requirements (deployment)
Answer: an SLA or uptime target. 99.9 percent can usually be met in one AZ with good recovery; 99.99 percent usually needs multiple AZs and load balancing; a regional-failure requirement needs multi-region.

Question: Compliance requirements (deployment)
Answer: data residency, audit logging, certified services. They often decide the region before anything else.

Question: Network requirements (deployment)
Answer: bandwidth, latency, connectivity to on premises (VPN or dedicated connection), IP ranges that must not overlap.

Question: Compute requirements (deployment)
Answer: VM, container or serverless, CPU architecture, GPU need, licensing that requires dedicated hosts.

Question: Collection (operations)
Answer: getting logs off the source. Agents on VMs (the CloudWatch agent, Azure Monitor Agent, Fluent Bit, Filebeat) read files and system journals and ship them. Managed services usually emit logs natively, but you often have to switch them on, for example load balancer access logs or storage access logs.

Question: Aggregation (operations)
Answer: bringing logs from many sources into one place, in one format, so you can search and correlate them. A single request may touch a load balancer, three microservices and a database; without aggregation you would log in to each one. The ELK stack (Elasticsearch, Logstash, Kibana), Splunk, AWS CloudWatch Logs, Azure Monitor Logs (Log Analytics) and Google Cloud Logging all aggregate.

Question: Retention (operations)
Answer: how long logs are kept, and where. Retention is set by regulation, contract and internal policy, then balanced against cost. Keep recent logs in a fast, searchable store and move older logs to cheap object or archive storage. PCI DSS, for example, requires at least one year of audit log history with the last three months immediately available.

Question: Metrics (operations)
Answer: numeric time series. Infrastructure metrics include CPU, memory, disk IOPS and network throughput. Application metrics include request rate, error rate and latency. Business metrics include orders per minute.

Question: Baseline (operations)
Answer: the normal range for a metric. You cannot judge "high" without knowing normal, and baselines also matter for security in Domain 4.

Question: Triage (operations)
Answer: deciding how serious an alert is and who owns it. Use severity levels (for example, critical pages the on-call engineer now; warning opens a ticket for business hours). Group related alerts so one outage does not produce two hundred pages.

Question: Response (operations)
Answer: what happens next. Every alert should link to a runbook. Some responses can be automated: restart a failed service, scale out, isolate a compromised instance. Escalate if nobody acknowledges within a set time.

Question: Vertical scaling (scale up or down) (operations)
Answer: make one instance bigger or smaller: more vCPU or memory. Simple, works for applications that cannot be split, but has a ceiling (the largest instance size) and usually needs a restart.

Question: Horizontal scaling (scale out or in) (operations)
Answer: add or remove instances behind a load balancer. Practically no ceiling, adds redundancy, and does not need a restart. It requires the application to be stateless, or to keep session state in a shared store such as a cache or database.

Question: Triggered by trend (operations)
Answer: scaling based on a pattern over time, often called predictive scaling. The system learns that load rises every weekday at 08:00 and adds capacity ahead of it.

Question: Triggered by load (operations)
Answer: reactive scaling on a live metric crossing a threshold, such as average CPU above 70 percent or queue depth above 1,000 messages. This is classic auto scaling. Use cooldown periods so the group does not flap up and down.

Question: Triggered by event (operations)
Answer: scaling in response to a specific event, such as a message arriving, a file landing in storage or an external webhook. Serverless platforms and event-driven autoscalers (for example KEDA on Kubernetes) work this way.

Question: Scheduled (operations)
Answer: scaling at known times set by a calendar: scale out before the 09:00 Monday rush, scale in at night, add capacity for a planned product launch.

Question: Manual (operations)
Answer: an operator changes the capacity by hand. Fine for one-off changes; poor as a strategy because humans are slow and forget to scale back in.

Question: Full (operations)
Answer: copies everything selected, every time. Simplest and fastest to restore (one set), but slowest to run and uses the most storage.

Question: Incremental (operations)
Answer: copies only what changed since the last backup of any type. Fastest and smallest to run. To restore you need the last full plus every incremental since, in order, so restore is slower and a single missing increment breaks the chain.

Question: Differential (operations)
Answer: copies everything changed since the last full backup. Each differential grows through the week. To restore you need the last full plus only the latest differential.

Question: On-site backup (operations)
Answer: kept in the same location (or region) as the data. Fast to restore, but lost in the same disaster.

Question: Off-site backup (operations)
Answer: kept in another location, region or account. Survives site loss and, if in a separate account with restricted access, survives an attacker who controls the main account.

Question: Schedule (operations)
Answer: how often backups run. The schedule is set by the RPO: if the business can lose at most four hours of data, backups (or replication) must happen at least every four hours.

Question: Replication (operations)
Answer: copying backups (or live data) to a second location automatically. Cross-region backup copy is the cloud form of off-site.

Question: Encryption (operations)
Answer: backups contain the same sensitive data as production, so encrypt them at rest and in transit, and manage the keys so that a lost key does not make every backup useless.

Question: Recoverability (operations)
Answer: can you actually restore? Run regular test restores into an isolated environment and time them against the RTO.

Question: Integrity (operations)
Answer: is the restored data correct and complete? Check checksums, row counts and that the application starts and reads the data.

Question: In-place recovery (operations)
Answer: restore over the original resource, replacing its current contents. Quick and keeps addresses and names, but destroys whatever was there, so you cannot compare or fall back.

Question: Parallel recovery (operations)
Answer: restore to a new resource alongside the original (a new volume, a new database instance). You can verify the restored data, copy back only what you need, and keep the original for forensics. Slower to cut over because names and connections must be repointed.

Question: Bulk recovery (operations)
Answer: restore an entire system, volume or database at once. Right after a disaster or full corruption.

Question: Granular recovery (operations)
Answer: restore a single item: one file, one mailbox, one table or one object version. Right when a user deleted one thing.

Question: Patch (operations)
Answer: a small fix for a bug or security vulnerability, often urgent. Security patches for actively exploited vulnerabilities should go out quickly, within days.

Question: Minor update (operations)
Answer: a backward-compatible release with fixes and small features, such as 2.3 to 2.4. Low risk, but still tested.

Question: Major update (operations)
Answer: a release that can break compatibility, such as a new database major version, an OS upgrade or a Kubernetes version jump. Needs planning, testing, sometimes code changes, and a rollback plan.

Question: Ephemeral data (operations)
Answer: data that exists only for the life of the resource: an instance store disk, a container's writable layer, a temporary scratch directory. It is lost on stop, termination or replacement.

Question: Persistent data (operations)
Answer: data on storage that outlives the compute: block volumes set to persist, file shares, object storage, databases.

Question: End of life (EOL) (operations)
Answer: the vendor stops selling and developing the product. It may still get some fixes for a time.

Question: End of support (EOS) (operations)
Answer: the vendor stops providing patches, security fixes and help. Running past end of support means unpatched vulnerabilities and often a compliance failure.

Question: Scanning scope (security)
Answer: deciding what to scan: which accounts, networks, hosts, container images, code repositories and managed services. A scan that misses a forgotten subnet gives false comfort. Scope also has a legal side: scanning provider infrastructure you do not own may break the provider's terms, so check their penetration testing policy.

Question: Identification (security)
Answer: running the scanners (authenticated host scanners, image scanners in the registry, dependency scanners in the pipeline, cloud configuration scanners) and collecting findings.

Question: Assessment (security)
Answer: deciding which findings matter. Severity scores are a start, but context decides priority: is the system internet facing, is there a known exploit, does it hold sensitive data, is there a compensating control?

Question: Remediation (security)
Answer: fixing the issue (patch, upgrade, configuration change) or, when a fix is not possible yet, mitigating it (block the port, add a WAF rule) and accepting the remaining risk formally. Then rescan to confirm.

Question: Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVE) (security)
Answer: the public catalogue of known vulnerabilities, each with an ID such as CVE-2021-44228 (Log4Shell). Scanners report findings by CVE ID.

Question: Common Vulnerability Scoring System (CVSS) (security)
Answer: the 0 to 10 severity score attached to a CVE. 9.0 and above is critical.

Question: Common Weakness Enumeration (CWE) (security)
Answer: the catalogue of weakness types (for example SQL injection, CWE-89) that cause vulnerabilities. CVE is a specific instance; CWE is the class.

Question: Data sovereignty (security)
Answer: data is subject to the laws of the country where it is stored or processed. A government may be able to demand access to data held in its territory.

Question: Data ownership (security)
Answer: who is accountable for a dataset and decides how it is used, classified and shared. Usually a business owner, not IT. In cloud, the customer owns its data; the provider is a processor.

Question: Data locality (residency) (security)
Answer: where data physically sits. Regulations or contracts may require that data stays in a country or region, which you meet by choosing regions and restricting replication and backup copies.

Question: Data classification (security)
Answer: labelling data by sensitivity (for example public, internal, confidential, restricted) so the right controls apply. Classification drives encryption, access and DLP rules.

Question: Data retention (security)
Answer: how long data must be kept and when it must be deleted.

Question: Litigation hold (legal hold) (security)
Answer: an instruction to preserve data relevant to a lawsuit or investigation, overriding normal deletion schedules. Object lock or legal hold features in cloud storage enforce it.

Question: Contractual retention (security)
Answer: retention required by agreements with customers or partners.

Question: Regulatory retention (security)
Answer: retention required by law or regulation, such as financial records rules.

Question: SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2) (security)
Answer: an independent auditor's report on a service organization's controls against the trust services criteria: security, availability, processing integrity, confidentiality and privacy. A Type I report covers design at a point in time; a Type II report covers how controls operated over a period, usually 6 to 12 months. Customers ask providers for SOC 2 Type II reports.

Question: PCI DSS (Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard) (security)
Answer: required for anyone who stores, processes or transmits payment card data. Scope reduction (segmenting the cardholder data environment, or using a payment provider's hosted page so card numbers never touch your systems) is the main design lever.

Question: ISO/IEC 27001 (security)
Answer: the international standard for an information security management system (ISMS). Organizations are certified against it by an accredited body after an audit.

Question: Cloud Security Alliance (CSA) (security)
Answer: a non-profit that publishes the Cloud Controls Matrix (CCM), the Consensus Assessments Initiative Questionnaire (CAIQ) and the STAR registry, where providers publish their security self-assessments and certifications.

Question: Programmatic access (security)
Answer: automation and code calling the provider's APIs.

Question: API (security)
Answer: direct HTTPS calls, signed with keys or tokens.

Question: SDK (security)
Answer: language libraries (Python, Java, .NET, Go) that wrap the API and handle signing and retries.

Question: CLI (security)
Answer: command-line tools such as the AWS CLI, Azure CLI and gcloud. (CompTIA's acronym list expands CLI as "Common Language Infrastructure", which is a quirk; in this context it means the command-line interface.)

Question: Web portal (security)
Answer: the browser console. It should require MFA and, for admins, ideally single sign-on through the corporate identity provider.

Question: Secure Shell (SSH) (security)
Answer: encrypted remote shell for Linux, using key pairs rather than passwords.

Question: Remote Desktop Protocol (RDP) (security)
Answer: graphical remote access to Windows on TCP 3389.

Question: Bastion host (jump box) (security)
Answer: a hardened host in a public subnet that admins connect to first, then hop to private instances. It narrows the exposed surface to one well-monitored machine. Managed equivalents (Azure Bastion, AWS Systems Manager Session Manager, Google IAP TCP forwarding) remove the need to open SSH or RDP to the internet at all.

Question: Local users (security)
Answer: accounts created directly in the cloud account or on the server. Simple but hard to manage at scale, and they are not removed when someone leaves the company unless a person remembers.

Question: Federation (security)
Answer: trusting an external identity provider (IdP) so users sign in with their corporate identity. Joiners and leavers are handled once, centrally.

Question: SAML (Security Assertion Markup Language) (security)
Answer: an XML-based federation standard. The IdP sends a signed assertion to the service provider. Common for enterprise single sign-on to consoles and SaaS.

Question: Token-based (security)
Answer: after authentication the client gets a token (often a JSON Web Token) and presents it with each request. Tokens expire, which limits the damage if one leaks.

Question: Directory-based (security)
Answer: authentication against a directory service such as Active Directory or LDAP. Microsoft Entra ID is the cloud directory behind Azure and Microsoft 365.

Question: Multifactor authentication (MFA) (security)
Answer: two or more different factor types: something you know (password), something you have (authenticator app, hardware key) or something you are (biometric). Two passwords is not MFA. Phishing-resistant MFA uses hardware security keys or passkeys (FIDO2).

Question: OpenID Connect (OIDC) (security)
Answer: an identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 using JSON tokens. Common for modern web and mobile sign-in and for letting CI/CD pipelines obtain cloud credentials without stored secrets.

Question: Role-based access control (RBAC) (security)
Answer: permissions are attached to roles (for example "network admin" or "read-only auditor") and users or workloads take on roles. Scales well and maps to job functions.

Question: Group-based access control (security)
Answer: permissions attached to groups and users added to groups. In practice groups are often mapped to roles.

Question: OAuth 2.0 (security)
Answer: a delegated authorization framework. A user lets an application act on their behalf with limited scopes ("read calendar") without giving the application their password. OAuth is authorization; OIDC adds authentication on top.

Question: Discretionary access control (DAC) (security)
Answer: the owner of a resource decides who gets access, as with file permissions or sharing a document. Flexible but hard to govern.

Question: Audit trail (security)
Answer: an immutable record of who did what, when, from where. Control-plane audit logs (AWS CloudTrail, Azure Activity Log, Google Cloud Audit Logs) are the cloud's audit trail. Protect them by sending them to a separate, locked-down account.

Question: Zero Trust (security)
Answer: never trust based on network location; verify every request using identity, device health and context, grant the least access needed, and assume breach. In practice: strong identity with MFA, micro-segmentation, encryption everywhere, continuous monitoring.

Question: Hardening (security)
Answer: reducing attack surface: remove unused software and accounts, close unused ports, disable default credentials, apply benchmark settings, and build from a hardened golden image.

Question: Patching (security)
Answer: applying security fixes promptly. Covered in Operations; from a security view the point is speed for exploited vulnerabilities.

Question: Encryption of data in transit (security)
Answer: TLS 1.2 or 1.3 for web and API traffic, IPsec for site-to-site VPNs, SSH for admin sessions.

Question: Encryption of data at rest (security)
Answer: AES-256 for disks, databases, object storage and backups. Keys live in a key management service (AWS KMS, Azure Key Vault, Google Cloud KMS) or a hardware security module. Customer-managed keys give you control of rotation and revocation.

Question: Secrets management (security)
Answer: store passwords, API keys and certificates in a secrets manager (AWS Secrets Manager, Azure Key Vault, Google Secret Manager, HashiCorp Vault), fetch them at runtime, rotate them automatically, and never commit them to source control.

Question: API security (security)
Answer: authenticate every call, authorize per resource, validate input, rate limit, use TLS, and log access. An API gateway centralizes these controls. The OWASP API Security Top 10 lists common mistakes such as broken object-level authorization.

Question: Principle of least privilege (security)
Answer: give each identity only the permissions it needs, for only as long as it needs them. Start with nothing and add; review and remove unused permissions.

Question: Container security (security)
Answer: run containers as unprivileged (non-root) users; avoid privileged mode, which gives the container near-host-level access to the kernel and devices. Set file access permissions tightly inside the image, use read-only root file systems where possible, scan images for CVEs and use minimal base images.

Question: Storage security (security)
Answer: for object storage, block public access at the account level, use bucket policies and encryption, enable versioning and object lock against deletion. For file storage, restrict network access to known subnets, use share and file permissions and encrypt.

Question: Endpoint protection (security)
Answer: anti-malware and endpoint detection and response (EDR) agents on VMs and workstations. They catch malware and suspicious process behaviour that network controls cannot see.

Question: Data loss prevention (DLP) (security)
Answer: tools that discover and classify sensitive data (card numbers, health records, personal data) and block or alert when it moves where it should not, such as to a public bucket or a personal email.

Question: Intrusion detection system (IDS) (security)
Answer: watches traffic or host activity and alerts on attacks. Passive.

Question: Intrusion prevention system (IPS) (security)
Answer: sits inline and blocks attacks as well as detecting them. Active, so a false positive can block legitimate traffic.

Question: DDoS protection (security)
Answer: absorbs and filters floods of traffic. Providers include basic protection for free and sell advanced tiers (AWS Shield Advanced, Azure DDoS Protection, Google Cloud Armor) with application-layer mitigation and response support.

Question: IAM policies (security)
Answer: JSON (or similar) documents that grant or deny actions on resources. An explicit deny overrides any allow.

Question: Firewall (security)
Answer: filtering traffic by rules, in several forms

Question: Network access control list (ACL) (security)
Answer: subnet-level, stateless rules evaluated in number order, with both allow and deny. Because it is stateless you must allow return traffic (often the ephemeral port range 1024-65535) explicitly.

Question: Network security group (security)
Answer: instance or interface level, stateful rules. Return traffic is allowed automatically. AWS calls these security groups (allow rules only); Azure network security groups support both allow and deny with priorities.

Question: Web application firewall (WAF) (security)
Answer: Layer 7 inspection of HTTP requests that blocks SQL injection, cross-site scripting, bad bots and abusive rates. It sits in front of a load balancer, application gateway, API gateway or CDN.

Question: Event monitoring (security)
Answer: collecting and correlating security events (logins, IAM changes, API calls, firewall denies) in a SIEM or the provider's threat detection service (Amazon GuardDuty, Microsoft Defender for Cloud and Sentinel, Google Security Command Center).

Question: Deviation from the baseline (security)
Answer: spotting activity outside normal patterns: API calls from a new country, a spike in outbound data, an admin logging in at 03:00, a sudden surge of CPU on idle machines.

Question: Unnecessary open ports (security)
Answer: any listening port that is not needed is attack surface. Regular port scans and configuration checks find SSH, RDP, database ports or management interfaces exposed by mistake.

Question: Vulnerability exploitation through human error (security)
Answer: misconfigurations such as a public storage bucket, an over-permissive security group or a disabled log. Most cloud breaches start here.

Question: Vulnerability exploitation through outdated software (security)
Answer: attackers use known CVEs in unpatched systems. Signs include unusual processes and outbound connections from a server running an old version.

Question: Social engineering: phishing (security)
Answer: tricking users into giving up credentials or running malware, often through fake login pages. Signs include logins from unusual locations right after a phishing campaign. Phishing-resistant MFA is the strongest defence.

Question: Malware: ransomware (security)
Answer: encrypts data and demands payment, and increasingly steals data first. Signs include mass file changes, deletion of snapshots and backups, and new encryption keys. Defences are immutable, off-site backups and least privilege on backup deletion.

Question: DDoS (security)
Answer: floods of traffic that exhaust bandwidth, connections or application resources. Signs are sudden traffic spikes from many sources and rising error rates.

Question: Cryptojacking (security)
Answer: attackers run cryptocurrency miners on your compute, often after stealing keys. Signs are sustained high CPU or GPU on instances that should be idle, unexpected instances in unused regions, and a surprise bill.

Question: Zombie instances (security)
Answer: forgotten, unmanaged resources that keep running unpatched and unmonitored. They are an easy foothold. Inventory, tagging and decommissioning fix them.

Question: Metadata service abuse (security)
Answer: every cloud VM can query a local instance metadata service (169.254.169.254) for information including temporary role credentials. A server-side request forgery (SSRF) flaw in a web app can trick the server into fetching those credentials for the attacker. Defences are enforcing the session-token version of the metadata service (IMDSv2 on AWS), least-privilege instance roles and fixing SSRF.

Question: Version management (devops fundamentals)
Answer: keeping the full history of every file so you can see what changed, compare versions, tag releases (for example v2.4.0) and roll back to a known good state.

Question: Code commit (devops fundamentals)
Answer: saving a set of changes to the local repository as one snapshot with a message. Good commits are small and describe why the change was made.

Question: Code push (devops fundamentals)
Answer: sending local commits to the shared remote repository so others can see them. In Git, commit is local and push is remote; a commit that was never pushed is invisible to the team and to the pipeline.

Question: Branch management (devops fundamentals)
Answer: a branch is an independent line of development. Teams create a branch per feature or fix, keep main (or trunk) always releasable, and delete branches after merging. Branch protection rules stop direct pushes to main and require reviews and passing checks.

Question: Pull request (devops fundamentals)
Answer: a request to merge one branch into another, which opens a page for review, discussion and automated checks. GitLab calls it a merge request.

Question: Code review (devops fundamentals)
Answer: teammates read the change before it merges, catching bugs, security issues and design problems, and spreading knowledge. Automated checks (tests, linting, security scans) run alongside human review.

Question: Code merge (devops fundamentals)
Answer: combining the changes from one branch into another. If two branches changed the same lines, Git reports a merge conflict that a person must resolve.

Question: Automation (devops fundamentals)
Answer: the core idea. Every repeatable step (build, test, scan, package, deploy) runs without manual clicks, so it runs the same way every time and fast enough to do many times a day.

Question: Code integration (devops fundamentals)
Answer: merging developers' changes frequently and verifying them automatically, so conflicts and bugs are found while they are small.

Question: Code deployment (devops fundamentals)
Answer: releasing the built artifact to an environment, using the strategies from Domain 2 (blue-green, canary, rolling, in-place).

Question: Build (devops fundamentals)
Answer: compiling code, resolving dependencies and producing an artifact. The same artifact should be promoted from test to staging to production; rebuilding per environment risks shipping something you did not test.

Question: Testing (devops fundamentals)
Answer: automated unit tests (one function), integration tests (components together), end-to-end tests (a user journey) and performance tests. Fast tests run first so failures surface quickly.

Question: Security (devops fundamentals)
Answer: "shift left" by putting security checks in the pipeline: static application security testing (SAST), dependency and software composition analysis, secret scanning, container image scanning and IaC policy checks. A critical finding fails the build. This is often called DevSecOps.

Question: Workflow (devops fundamentals)
Answer: the defined sequence of stages and the rules that connect them: what triggers the pipeline (push, pull request, schedule, tag), which stages run in parallel, where approvals sit, and what happens on failure.

Question: VM images (devops fundamentals)
Answer: prebuilt machine images (golden images) with the OS, patches and application baked in, such as AWS AMIs, Azure managed images or Google Compute Engine images. Often built by HashiCorp Packer.

Question: Container images (devops fundamentals)
Answer: Docker or OCI images pushed to a registry.

Question: Packages (devops fundamentals)
Answer: software in an installable format: RPM (Red Hat Package Manager, for RHEL, Fedora and similar), Debian (.deb, for Debian and Ubuntu), ZIP archives (common for serverless function bundles and Windows) and tar archives (often compressed as .tar.gz on Linux).

Question: Flat files (devops fundamentals)
Answer: plain files such as configuration files, scripts, static website assets or compiled binaries copied directly.

Question: Public repositories (devops fundamentals)
Answer: open to anyone, such as Docker Hub public images, the public npm or PyPI registries, and public GitHub repos. Convenient, but a supply-chain risk: pin versions and scan what you pull.

Question: Private repositories (devops fundamentals)
Answer: access-controlled stores for your own artifacts and code, such as Amazon ECR, Azure Container Registry, Google Artifact Registry, JFrog Artifactory, Sonatype Nexus and private Git repos.

Question: REST (Representational State Transfer) (devops fundamentals)
Answer: an architectural style over HTTP. Resources have URLs (/orders/42) and are acted on with HTTP methods: GET reads, POST creates, PUT replaces, PATCH updates, DELETE deletes (which map to CRUD). Usually JSON payloads. Stateless: each request carries everything needed. The most common style for cloud and public APIs.

Question: SOAP (Simple Object Access Protocol) (devops fundamentals)
Answer: a protocol with strict XML message envelopes and a formal contract (WSDL). Heavier than REST but has built-in standards for security and reliability (WS-Security). Still common in banking, government and older enterprise systems.

Question: RPC (remote procedure call) (devops fundamentals)
Answer: calling a function on another machine as if it were local, such as getPrice(itemId). Modern RPC frameworks such as gRPC use HTTP/2 and Protocol Buffers for fast, strongly typed service-to-service calls, which suits internal microservice traffic.

Question: WebSockets (devops fundamentals)
Answer: a persistent, two-way connection between client and server over a single TCP connection, upgraded from HTTP. Either side can send at any time, which suits chat, live dashboards, multiplayer games and notifications. REST, by contrast, needs the client to ask (polling).

Question: GraphQL (devops fundamentals)
Answer: a query language for APIs where the client asks for exactly the fields it needs in one request to a single endpoint. It avoids over-fetching (getting fields you do not need) and under-fetching (needing several REST calls to build one screen). Useful for mobile apps and front ends that aggregate many data sources.

Question: Ansible (devops fundamentals)
Answer: agentless configuration management and automation from Red Hat. Playbooks written in YAML describe tasks that run over SSH (or WinRM for Windows). Idempotent modules make re-runs safe. Use it to configure servers, install software and orchestrate multi-step operations. Configuration as code.

Question: Docker (devops fundamentals)
Answer: builds, ships and runs containers. A Dockerfile defines the image layers; docker build creates the image, docker push sends it to a registry, docker run starts a container. Docker Compose runs multi-container apps on one host.

Question: ELK stack (devops fundamentals)
Answer: Elasticsearch (search and analytics engine that stores and indexes data), Logstash (ingests, parses and transforms logs) and Kibana (dashboards and search UI). Together they centralize and search logs. Lightweight Beats shippers often replace or feed Logstash. OpenSearch is a fork with the same roles.

Question: Git (devops fundamentals)
Answer: the distributed version control system underneath GitHub, GitLab and Bitbucket. Every clone holds the full history.

Question: GitHub Actions (devops fundamentals)
Answer: CI/CD built into GitHub. Workflows are YAML files in .github/workflows/ that run jobs on runners when events happen (push, pull request, schedule, release).

Question: Grafana (devops fundamentals)
Answer: dashboards and visualization for metrics, logs and traces from many data sources, such as Prometheus, Elasticsearch and cloud monitoring services. It also does alerting. Grafana displays data; it is not usually the store.

Question: Jenkins (devops fundamentals)
Answer: a long-established, self-hosted, open-source automation server for CI/CD. Pipelines are defined in a Jenkinsfile. Very flexible, with a huge plugin ecosystem, but you run and patch the server and its agents yourself.

Question: Kubernetes (devops fundamentals)
Answer: the container orchestration platform. It schedules pods across nodes, restarts failed containers, scales with the Horizontal Pod Autoscaler, rolls out updates through Deployments, provides service discovery through Services, and is configured with YAML manifests. Managed as EKS, AKS and GKE.

Question: Terraform (devops fundamentals)
Answer: HashiCorp's declarative infrastructure as code tool. HCL files describe resources across many providers; terraform plan previews changes and terraform apply makes them. It tracks what it built in a state file, which should be stored remotely with locking so two people cannot apply at once. Multi-cloud, unlike CloudFormation (AWS only) or Bicep (Azure only). OpenTofu is an open-source fork.

Question: Resource allocation (troubleshooting)
Answer: not enough CPU, memory, disk or IP addresses assigned, or a Kubernetes pod requesting more than any node can provide (the pod stays Pending). Container limits set too low cause OOM kills (OOMKilled, exit code 137).

Question: Permission issues (troubleshooting)
Answer: the deployment identity lacks rights to create a resource, read a secret or pass a role to a service. Look for "AccessDenied", "Forbidden", "AuthorizationFailed" or HTTP 403 in the deployment logs. Fix by granting the specific missing permission, not by making the pipeline an administrator.

Question: Oversubscription (troubleshooting)
Answer: more virtual resources are promised than physical resources exist, such as too many vCPUs per physical core on a private cloud host or too many VMs on a datastore. Symptoms include high CPU ready or steal time and storage latency even though each VM looks lightly used.

Question: Sizing issues (troubleshooting)
Answer: the instance type or volume is too small (performance problems, failed health checks under load) or too large (wasted money). Also includes choosing a type that does not support a needed feature, such as a GPU or enhanced networking.

Question: Full outage (troubleshooting)
Answer: the service is completely unavailable to everyone. Check provider status pages, DNS, certificates, load balancer health and the most recent change. Fail over to another region if the design allows.

Question: Partial outage (troubleshooting)
Answer: some users, some features or some regions are affected, or the service is degraded but up. Narrow the scope: which AZ, which instance group, which version (a bad canary), which client type. Partial outages are harder to spot and are where good monitoring and tracing pay off.

Question: API throttling (troubleshooting)
Answer: the provider limits how many API calls per second an account or caller may make. Too many calls return HTTP 429 (Too Many Requests) or errors such as "Rate exceeded" or "ThrottlingException". Fix with exponential backoff and jitter on retries, caching, batching calls, and spreading automation over time.

Question: Service quotas (troubleshooting)
Answer: per-account or per-region limits on resources such as the number of vCPUs, VPCs, elastic IPs or load balancers. When reached, creation fails with "LimitExceeded" or "QuotaExceeded". Request an increase in advance, especially before a launch or a DR failover into a region where you normally run little.

Question: DNS (troubleshooting)
Answer: turns names into addresses. Symptoms are "could not resolve host" or connections going to an old address. Causes include wrong or missing records, TTL caching after a change, a private hosted zone not associated with the VPC, split-horizon confusion, or a resolver that cannot be reached on port 53 UDP and TCP.

Question: NTP (troubleshooting)
Answer: keeps clocks in sync. Clock drift breaks things that depend on time: Kerberos authentication (fails beyond 5 minutes of skew by default), TLS certificate validation, signed API requests (cloud APIs reject requests whose timestamp is too far off) and log correlation. Symptom: authentication errors that make no sense, or "request expired" or "signature not yet valid".

Question: NAT (troubleshooting)
Answer: lets private instances reach the internet using a shared public address. If a private subnet cannot reach the internet (package installs time out), check that its route table sends 0.0.0.0/0 to a NAT gateway, that the NAT gateway sits in a public subnet with an internet gateway route, and that the NAT gateway is healthy. NAT gateways can also run out of ports under very high connection counts.

Question: HTTP status codes (troubleshooting)
Answer: the response code tells you which side failed.

Question: Latency (troubleshooting)
Answer: delay. Causes include geographic distance, too many hops, cross-region or cross-AZ calls in a chatty application, VPN over a congested internet path, and DNS lookups. Fix by moving compute closer to users or data, using a CDN, keeping chatty tiers in one AZ, or using a dedicated connection.

Question: Bandwidth or throughput issues (troubleshooting)
Answer: not enough capacity. Causes include an instance type with low network bandwidth, a saturated VPN tunnel (one IPsec tunnel often tops out around 1.25 Gbps on major providers), a NAT gateway or firewall bottleneck, and MTU mismatches that cause fragmentation (VPN tunnels need a smaller MTU because of encapsulation overhead).

Question: Protocol incompatibility (troubleshooting)
Answer: two ends cannot agree: IKEv1 on one VPN peer and IKEv2 only on the other, mismatched encryption or Diffie-Hellman groups in VPN phase 1 or 2, HTTP/2 or gRPC through a proxy that only speaks HTTP/1.1, IPv6-only clients reaching an IPv4-only service, or SMB versions that do not overlap.

Question: Protocol deprecations (troubleshooting)
Answer: old protocols turned off for security: SSLv3, TLS 1.0 and 1.1, SMBv1, older SSH key types. A legacy client that only supports a deprecated protocol suddenly fails after a server or provider update. Fix by upgrading the client, not by re-enabling the weak protocol.

Question: Scope exhaustion (troubleshooting)
Answer: the DHCP scope or subnet has no free addresses left. New instances, pods or containers fail to launch with "insufficient free addresses". In cloud subnets remember the provider reserves some addresses (AWS reserves five per subnet), and Kubernetes pod networking can consume one VPC address per pod. Fix by adding a larger or additional subnet or CIDR block, and size subnets with growth in mind.

Question: Network overlap (troubleshooting)
Answer: two networks use the same address range, so they cannot be routed to each other. You cannot peer two VPCs whose CIDR blocks overlap, and a VPN to an on-premises network that also uses 10.0.0.0/16 will not route. Prevention is an IP address management (IPAM) plan before you build. Fixes after the fact include re-addressing or NAT between the overlapping networks.

Question: Missing routes (troubleshooting)
Answer: the route table has no entry for the destination, so traffic goes nowhere or out the default route. Classic cases: a VPC peering connection was accepted but neither side added a route; a new subnet was associated with the wrong route table; a VPN is up but the on-premises CIDR was never added or propagated.

Question: Misconfigured routes (troubleshooting)
Answer: the route exists but points to the wrong target, such as a private subnet's default route pointing at an internet gateway (instances without public IPs then cannot reach the internet at all) or an overlapping, more specific route sending traffic the wrong way. Remember the longest prefix match wins.

Question: Misconfigured VLAN tags (troubleshooting)
Answer: a VM's port group or a physical switch port is tagged with the wrong VLAN ID, so the host lands in the wrong network. It gets no DHCP address or the wrong one, and cannot reach its gateway.

Question: Authorization issues: unauthorized access (troubleshooting)
Answer: someone reaches data or resources they should not, often through a misconfiguration such as a public bucket, a share link, an overly broad role or a security group open to the world. Contain first (remove the public access, revoke sessions), then investigate with access logs, then fix the policy and add a guardrail so it cannot recur.

Question: Software vulnerability issues (troubleshooting)
Answer: a scanner or advisory reports a CVE in an OS package, library or container image. Assess exposure, patch or upgrade, rebuild images, redeploy, then rescan. If no patch exists, mitigate with a WAF rule, network restriction or configuration change.

Question: Unauthorized software (troubleshooting)
Answer: software installed outside policy, such as a cryptominer, a remote access tool, an unapproved database or an unlicensed product. Found by endpoint agents, software inventory and process monitoring. Remove it, find how it was installed, and enforce allow-lists or golden images with no interactive admin access.
